Vesuvius Challenge · First Letters

Scroll Scout

Before anyone spends GPU time on a Herculaneum scroll, Scroll Scout predicts whether a seed point will give a clean papyrus surface, and checks whether a segment that has already been traced stays on its sheet, from a few megabytes of public CT data, on a laptop CPU. It passes three independent tests and maps all 21 scrolls still eligible for the $50,000 First Letters prizes.

20/20of the team's own segments called right by check-segment, on two scrolls never used to build it (AUC 1.00)
0.88held-out AUC on 65 judged survey patches
21unread scrolls mapped, 4,224 points scored
4.5 sper point on one CPU core; no GPU, no downloads beyond the chunks it reads

The problem

Every attempt to read an unread scroll starts by growing a surface on one papyrus sheet inside the CT scan, then running an ink model on it. In crushed parts of a scroll the sheets touch and fuse, the grown surface jumps between them, and the ink model sees noise. In the First Letters survey, only 12 of 65 automatically grown patches on the eligible scrolls stayed on their sheet over most of their area. Ink inference on the rest is wasted.

What the scout sees

Around a point, Scroll Scout reads a 3.3 mm cube of the CT and of the published surface-m7 prediction at pyramid level 1 (17 µm voxels) and measures five things: are the predicted sheets flat, unfused and unfragmented, and does the sheet orientation, in the prediction and in the raw CT, avoid swirling?

Does it work?

Three independent tests, each against labels nobody made for this tool.

Survey patches

Ground truth is the survey's verdict for each of its 65 patches: did the grown surface stay on the sheet? 12 did. The score was tested two ways.

scoreAUC95% CItop-10 precision
no ranking (the survey’s grid of seeds)0.50–18%
v1, terms fixed before looking at results0.84 0.72–0.9350%
v2, leave-one-scroll-out0.88 0.78–0.9550%

Leave-one-scroll-out means: for each of the 21 scrolls, the signals were chosen using the other 20 only, then tested on the held-out scroll. The same four signals were chosen in all 21 rounds. Both results have a permutation p-value of 0.0002. Scored over each patch's whole surface with check-segment (12 points per patch rather than the seed alone), the AUC is 0.85 (0.74–0.94); the score was tuned on these patches, so this is a consistency check rather than a new test.

The team's own segments

The team published 21 automatically grown segments for PHerc. 800 and PHerc. 1447, and the survey judged each: 9 follow the sheet, 11 cut obliquely across several layers, 1 is mixed. Neither scroll was used to choose or calibrate the score. Scoring 12 points over each segment, every segment that follows the sheet scores above every one that cuts across layers: AUC 1.00, permutation p = 0.0002. Within PHerc. 1447 alone (3 good, 11 bad) the separation is also perfect (AUC 1.00, p = 0.0014).

Check a segment before ink detection

This test is exactly what scrollscout check-segment does with any traced segment: a tifxyz folder, an OBJ mesh or an open-data URL. Its rule was fixed before the test: a segment likely follows the sheet when its median point scores above the clean threshold set on the survey (0.63). That rule gets 20 of 20 segments right; the survey's one mixed segment comes out as likely to cut across layers. It takes about 15 seconds on 4 CPU cores, against hours of GPU time for ink detection, and draws a map of where the segment runs into crushed papyrus.

Every published segment, checked

check-segment ran on every segment in the open-data bucket it can check: the 81 segments, on 5 scrolls, with a tifxyz mesh traced on an 8.6–9.4 µm scan that has a published surface prediction. 45 of 81 likely follow their sheet. Outside the 20 segments the survey judged, these verdicts are predictions: a way to decide which segments to run ink detection on, or train on, first. The full list is census/SEGMENTS.md in the repository. The 46 segments of PHerc. 500P2 were not checked: they sit on a 2.215 µm scan, outside the scans the score was validated on.

Where text was actually found

Two scrolls on the same 8.64 µm, 116 keV scan protocol as most eligible scrolls have produced text: PHerc. 343, whose 18 letters won the October First Letters prize, and PHerc. 1447, where the team found text in September. The scout scored those exact places against random points inside the same scrolls.

The atlas

128 points were spread through each of the 21 eligible scroll volumes (8 heights × 4 distances from the axis) and scored; PHerc. 125, PHerc. 175A, PHerc. 306B, PHerc. 483A got 512 points each for their seeds. Scrolls are ranked by their best 10% of points from the even pass. The seed shown is each scroll's best point in its inner part (within 0.45 of the way from the axis to the outside, away from the top and bottom 15%), where both known text finds lie, as level-0 voxel coordinates (x y z) of the eligible volume. Copy puts a ready-to-run fls.py command on the clipboard. More seeds per scroll, inner and overall, are in atlas/seeds.csv.

Use it

pip install "git+https://github.com/tkran2/scrollscout"
scrollscout point PHerc1447 20250521151220 4144 2742 12557     # score one point (x y z)
scrollscout near  PHerc1447 20250521151220 4144 2742 12557     # best seeds around a target
scrollscout scan  PHerc0306B 20250521133212 --points 128        # map one scroll, pick seeds
scrollscout seeds PHerc0306B_20250521133212_scout.json          # seeds and fls.py commands
scrollscout export-vc3d PHerc0306B_20250521133212_scout.json    # colour-coded points for VC3D
scrollscout check-segment path/to/segment.tifxyz --png map.png  # does a traced segment stay on its sheet?
scrollscout atlas --out atlas/                                  # every First Letters volume

No GPU, no VC3D install and no full-volume downloads: the tool reads only the chunks it needs from s3://vesuvius-challenge-open-data. Source, tests and every script behind these numbers: https://github.com/tkran2/scrollscout.

Limits

All labels were judged by one person (the survey's author), and the team-segment test has 20 segments. Spiral fits and lasagna surfaces are untested. check-segment scores the papyrus a segment passes through, not the segment's own path, so a segment that jumps layers inside clean papyrus would pass. A clean surface is necessary for reading text, not sufficient: the scout says where tracing works, not where the ink is. Its seeds are the best of the sampled points, not the best in the scroll.

CT scans and surface predictions: Vesuvius Challenge open data (CC BY-NC 4.0); figures derived from them carry the same licence. Ground truth: First Letters survey by Matteo Bulloni. PHerc. 343 letter locations: Erwin Nieuwlaar's winning submission. Code: MIT.
